1:
Calvin sets out the logic before anything else. The chapter has three principal heads, and the first shows that Israel had no reason to be aggrieved at paying tithes to the Levites and first-fruits to the priests, since that tribe was deprived of its inheritance. God obviates all quarrels, and prevents unlawful gains and pilferings, by assigning each his just share. Since God was as it were the lot of their inheritance, the Levites justly claimed the right he had transferred to them; and if it were disagreeable to the people that their revenue should be tithed, God came as it were between, declaring the tithe his property in his right as King and appointing the Levites his stewards and collectors to receive it. There was then no ground for anyone to raise a dispute, unless he chose professedly to rob God. The declaration is often repeated, Calvin notes, so that the people might be assured God accounted as received by himself whatever he assigned to the Levites — not merely lest a portion be withheld, but that every man pay those dues willingly and none murmur. A second reason is added: God had appointed them the ministers of his service, and the labourer is worthy of his hire. Gill limits the exclusion to the division of Canaan; Wesley identifies 'his inheritance' as the Lord's own portion, the tithes and first-fruits distinct from what was made by fire.

Henry turns the law into a double caution, calling it a setting of land-marks between the estates of the priests and those of the people. Care is taken, first, that the priests should not entangle themselves with the affairs of this life nor enrich themselves with the wealth of this world, having better things to mind: no share in the spoils of war, none in the land divided by lot, their warfare and husbandry being both spiritual, and enough to fill their hands with work and profit and to content them. Hence the note the passage is best known for — those who have God for their inheritance should not be greedy of great things in the world, neither gripe what they have nor grasp at more, but look on all present things with the indifference which becomes those who believe God all-sufficient. But care is taken also that they want none of the comforts of this life; for though God, who is a Spirit, is their inheritance, it does not follow that they must live upon the air. The people must provide for them, and their maintenance must rest not on generosity but on law: he that is taught in the word ought in justice to communicate to him that teaches him, and he that has the benefit of solemn assemblies ought to support those who preside in them.

Keil and Delitzsch treat the passage as deliberate repetition rather than fresh legislation. Moses repeats verbatim the essential part of the rule already laid down in Numbers, and the phrase 'all the tribe of Levi' takes in priests and Levites together. The inheritance of Jehovah which they were to eat consisted of the holy gifts as well as the sacrifices — the tithes, firstlings and first-fruits — described in detail there. Moses felt it superfluous to enumerate them, or to define how much fell to the priests and how much to the Levites; and Keil and Delitzsch resist the critical inference drawn from that silence, that the author was unacquainted with the distinction. Clarke adds two notes from the same angle: Maimonides understood the exclusion to mean no part in the spoils taken from an enemy, and the Lord being their inheritance means he is the portion of their souls, while as to their bodies they live by the offerings made by fire, whatever was the Lord's right in these being given by him to the priests.
3:
The due itself is small and exactly specified, and the witnesses spend their attention on what the three pieces are. Gill notes first who owes them: not the priests, as Jarchi observes, but those who bring the sacrifices to the priests, and particularly the peace offerings. Clarke reads the obligation more widely, because the word for sacrifice is used not only of an animal offered to the Lord but of one killed for common use; taking it in that sense, the command covers what the people were to allow the priests out of animals slain for their own table. He itemizes: the shoulder, probably cut off with the skin on, as Maimonides has it; the two cheeks, which may include the whole head; and the maw, the intestines commonly used for food. Keil and Delitzsch identify the parts technically — the shoulder is the front leg, and the maw is the rough stomach, the fourth stomach of ruminants where digestion is completed, the omasus of the Latins, though the Vulgate has ventriculus. On why these three, they report Münster and Fagius: the animal has three principal parts, head, feet and trunk, and some portion of each went to the officiating priest. Wesley alone leaves it open, noting that the Hebrew rendered maw may have another signification, some rendering it the breast and others the part lying beneath it.

Calvin asks why God troubles to enumerate the portions at all, and answers that the list protects both parties. It is not only for the sake of the priests that God says what he would have them receive, so that they may obtain what is their own without murmuring or dispute; he also has regard to the people, lest the priests should basely and greedily take more than their due. That this was no imaginary danger the sons of Eli show, who advanced to such licentiousness that, like robbers, they seized violently on whatever their lust desired. Lest the priesthood give way to that covetousness, God prescribes limits they were to keep within — with the consequence Calvin thinks worth naming, that if they transgressed them any of the people could easily convict them of avarice.

On the first-fruits the notes are brief and complementary. Gill identifies the offering by its technical name as the terumah, the heave offering of the first-fruits, and observes that the measure or quantity is not declared in the law itself but was afterwards fixed by the Jews. Clarke states the principle behind the transfer: all these first-fruits and firstlings were the Lord's portion, and these he gave to the priests. Keil and Delitzsch note that Moses is repeating the law of first-fruits already given in Numbers, and that he repeats it here for a particular purpose, to extend it to the first produce of the sheep-shearing. They then take up the ground of the right: the priests receive because the Lord chose them to stand and minister in his name on behalf of all the tribes — which means not merely by his appointment but in his power, as mediators of his grace. The words 'he and his sons', they add, point back quite to the Mosaic times, in which Aaron and his sons held the priest's office; and Gill reads the choosing as the choosing of the whole tribe of Levi out of all the other tribes of Israel.
6:
Keil and Delitzsch put the provision in line with what precedes: as the priests were remembered for their service on the part of the people, so the Levite who came from one of the towns with all the desire of his soul to the sanctuary was to eat a portion like all his brethren standing there in service. They correct a possible inference from 'sojourned' — it does not presuppose the Levites were houseless, only that they had no hereditary possession as the other tribes had, and lived as sojourners in the towns given up to them. 'All his brethren the Levites' means the priests together with the Levites officiating as their assistants, from which they conclude that only part of the tribe was engaged at the sanctuary at any one time. Gill fills in the background: the Levites were dispersed over the country, employed in teaching the people, and apart from their own cities were everywhere sojourners. On the portion he follows Jarchi — the newcomer had equal parts with the priests who usually ministered there, so that they divided the skins and flesh of the sin offerings, perhaps even those not coming by virtue of the feast.

Wesley reads the qualifying phrase as marking a voluntary act rather than a rota. To come with all the desire of his mind is to come with full purpose to fix his abode and spend his whole time and strength in the service of God; for the priests came to the temple by turns before David's time and certainly after it, and if any was not contented with that attendance but desired to devote himself more entirely, he was permitted — this being an eminent act of piety joined with self-denial, parting with the conveniences of his own city. Wesley then borrows a note written some sixty years before his own, and thinks it remarkable: a hearty, pious zeal to serve God and his church, though it encroach a little on a settled order and look irregular, ought to be gratified and not discouraged; he that loves dearly to be employed in the sanctuary, in God's name let him minister, and he shall be as welcome to God as those whose course it was.

Calvin treats this as the third head of the chapter, and says it explains more clearly what is elsewhere obscurely declared, since God had seemed to curtail from the Levites whatever he gave the priests. He now places the priests distinctly in the first rank, yet so that they should admit the Levites, on the score of their labours, to a share of the oblations. The sum is that Levites remaining at home should be content with tithes and touch nothing of the other offerings, but whenever they came to the sanctuary were to be accounted ministers and take their place: none excluded for the intermission of his duties, and those dwelling elsewhere no worse off than those at Jerusalem, since even there they did not cease from ministry, having duties besides sacrificing. Yet those who devoted themselves wholly to the sanctuary had double honour, for it was not just that they be defrauded of maintenance who bade adieu to domestic cares. On the patrimony clause the rest are brief. Ellicott takes it that the dedicated Levite had the same allowance from tithes as the others, beside the proceeds of his patrimony in his own city; Clarke draws from it what it implies about Levitical property, that though they had no part of the land by lot they were permitted to purchase houses, goods, cattle and even fields, as the cases of Abiathar and of Jeremiah show; and Wesley gives the reason twice over, that he who waited on the altar ought to live by the altar, and that it was fit he keep his money, wherewith to redeem what he had sold if he saw occasion.
9:
Calvin begins with the human tendency the command is written against. It is too well known how eagerly the human race lays hold of bad examples, and especially how readily those who come into a foreign land accustom themselves to its manners. This is why God commands them to beware lest on coming into Canaan they catch any infection from its inhabitants; the doctrine is universal, but the impending danger needed providing against. Calvin then finds in the verse a definition: Moses explains what it is to have other gods, namely to mix up the worship of God with things profane, since its purity is maintained only by banishing all uncongenial superstitions. The sum is that God's people should abstain from all the inventions of men whereby pure and simple religion is adulterated. In general God wished to deter his worshippers from every fallacy by which Satan has from the beginning deluded and fascinated miserable men, enumerating certain practices because these had obtained the greatest prevalence. Gill hears grace rather than warning in the opening clause, since the land is so often described as what the Lord thy God giveth thee, a mere favour without any desert of theirs, and so typical of the heavenly Canaan, the free gift of God through Christ.

Calvin goes further in asking what displeases God in these vices, and traces them to a faculty good in itself. Men have a natural desire after knowledge; even in the superstitious this proceeded from a good principle, God having implanted it in all when he would distinguish our race from the lower animals. Nor was it reprehensible that men, conscious of their ignorance, conceived they were to obtain knowledge only by consulting God. That was the sole object of the Gentiles when they inquired of magicians and sorcerers — to seek from heaven the knowledge they perceived themselves to lack; and in doing so they confessed that they were overwhelmed with darkness, and that the light of understanding is God's special gift. Calvin finds the confession preserved in the word itself: whence came the name of divination, since they were persuaded that secret things lay beyond human apprehension and such knowledge must come by divine inspiration. The fault lies in what the devil does with it, perverting by his machinations what is right in itself.

Henry is simply astonished that the warning was needed. One would not think there had been so much need as there was to arm Israel against the infection of Canaanite custom. Was it possible that a people so blessed with divine institutions should admit the brutish and barbarous inventions of men and devils? Were they in danger of making their tutors and directors in religion those whom God had made their captives and tributaries? It seems they were, and therefore, after many similar cautions, they are charged not to do after the abominations of those nations. Henry presses the same astonishment on his own readers: one would wonder that works of darkness so senseless and profane could be found where divine revelation shone so clearly, and yet remains of them survive even where Christ's religion is professed — such are the powers and policies of the rulers of the darkness of this world. Let those who give heed to fortune-tellers, or go to wizards for the discovery of things secret, or use spells for the cure of diseases, or keep any league with familiar spirits, know that they can have no fellowship with God while thus they have fellowship with devils. Keil and Delitzsch explain why the list that follows is so exhaustive: Moses groups together every word the language contained for exploring the future and discovering the will of God, so as to forbid soothsaying in all its descriptions — and puts the prohibition of Moloch-worship at their head to show the inward connection between soothsaying and idolatry.
10:
On the first prohibition the witnesses agree about the rite and differ on how far it went. Gill describes a lustration by fire: two fires were made and the child led between them by a priest, initiating him into Moloch's religion; besides this, he adds, they used to burn them. Clarke thinks the passing probably a consecration to Moloch or some other deity, and that their being burnt to death is not likely what the verse intends. Calvin allows both. This monstrous infatuation, which had possessed the Gentiles, afterwards invaded the Jews also, so that they immolated and even burnt their children in honour of the gods to which they had devoted them; though probably most were not inflamed to such madness, but satisfied their superstition by merely making them pass through the fire, a lustration to purge away all filthiness. Yet their cruel zeal impelled many even to murder, not sparing their own flesh and blood — and in that they pleaded Abraham's example, as if the obedience of that holy man, ready at God's command to slay his son, resembled this barbarous violence in people who murdered their children though God prohibited it. Calvin draws the lesson: men engage far more fervently in impious rites of their own devising than in worshipping God aright when he plainly enjoins what is good. It ought to be a parent's first care to consecrate his children to God — but the Jews' only rite of initiation was circumcision, and with that they should have been content.

Clarke works through the terms one by one, with the fullest glosses in the chapter. Divination he takes for the attempt to find out futurity by auguries and lots; the observer of times foretells events from present occurrences, predicting great changes from the aspects of the planets, eclipses and the motion of the clouds. The enchanter he derives from a root meaning to view attentively — one who inspected the entrails of beasts and observed the flight of birds, though some think divination by serpents is meant — and the witch is probably one who by drugs, herbs and perfumes pretended to bring celestial influences to her aid. The charmer uses spells — a peculiar conjunction, as the term implies, of words or things, tying knots for divination, a custom he finds in Virgil's shepherd. The consulter with familiar spirits is a Pythoness, inquiring by one spirit to get answers from another of superior order; and the necromancer inquires of the dead, like the witch at Endor, who professed to evoke them so that they might disclose the secrets of the spiritual world.

The others fill in what Clarke leaves, and one ventures a judgment on the whole list. Gill reports Aben Ezra and Ben Melech, who take divination for a general name whose particulars follow — a view Calvin says he does not disapprove, that Moses first uses a general term for all soothsayers and then proceeds to the kinds. Keil and Delitzsch explain the charmer as one who pronounced a ban, probably referring to the custom of binding by magical knots; Gill gives the rival accounts of that word — one who cures diseases by charms, a charmer of serpents, or, as Jarchi has it, one who gathers serpents and scorpions into one place, while Aben Ezra makes him one who says words to gather demons. Wesley reduces two terms to their plainest sense: the witch is one in covenant with the devil, the wizard a knowing man who by forbidden ways undertakes to reveal secret things. Ellicott notes that the word for charmer literally means one who ties knots, appears here for the first time in the Old Testament, and that four of these practices are ascribed to king Manasseh. He then adds the sentence that separates him from the rest: it is hardly possible that all were mere imposture and deceit.
12:
Gill narrows the reason clause: not that a man must do all these things, but whoever does any of them, as Jarchi notes — and with them all who consult such persons. It was especially abominable in Israel, who had the true God to consult, his law as the rule of their conduct, and his prophets to advise with in difficulties. Calvin sees two restraints at once. God would have his authority act as a rein; and he sets before them the vengeance he was soon to inflict on the heathen, of which they were themselves to be the ministers. Since the Canaanites were plainly rooted out by God's hand alone, he assigns as the cause their having polluted themselves and their country by these blasphemous superstitions — and by so striking an example deters Israel from imitating sins the facts showed to be thus punished, as Paul admonishes believers to shun what provokes God's wrath.

Against those practices stands one positive command, read here as a demand for undividedness rather than sinlessness. Gill glosses it as sincerely worshipping God, adhering to his word and walking uprightly; Wesley as being wholly his, cleaving to him and his word alone, and therefore abhorring all commerce with devils. Keil and Delitzsch note the Hebrew emphasis, the pronoun standing first as a nominative absolute — but thou, so far as thou art concerned, not so — and observe that though the heathen Israel exterminated hearkened to conjurers, Jehovah had allowed them nothing of the kind. Ellicott thinks Rashi's note worth preserving, and it is the most searching thing said on the verse: walk with him in sincerity and wait for him, pry not into the future, but whatsoever cometh upon thee take with simplicity, and thou shalt be his portion. Calvin grounds the demand in covenant: as God pledged himself to the Jews, so he made them his debtors, not to prostitute themselves to idols nor hanker after strange religions. The command opposes all mixtures which withdraw us from sincere worship, because the simplicity that keeps us obedient to heavenly teaching is the spiritual chastity God requires in his Church — which is why Paul is jealous over those he espoused to Christ, fearing lest, as the serpent beguiled Eve, they fall from it.

The last verse looks backward and forward. Calvin takes it as a condition on the inheritance: the land was given on these terms, that they be mindful of so great a benefit and beware of all pollutions, succeeding the former inhabitants with a view to being separate from them — for whence the change, except that God might acquire a new people and purify the land? Though only two classes of superstition are named, they indicate the whole: Israel was not to be like the nations in the vices that destroyed them, since God exterminated not only the men but their rites. Ellicott renders the clause more literally — as for thee, not so hath Jehovah thy God given unto thee — and finds a marked contrast between the miserable resources of idolatrous nations and the light promised to Israel and to us in the One Mediator. Even Israel was better off than the heathen: God had not left them to observers of times, having given the Shechinah to rest on the prophets, and the Urim and Thummim. Wesley adds the forward reference: God has instructed thee better by his word and spirit, and will instruct thee more fully by a great prophet. Keil and Delitzsch make that junction carry an argument. When Moses attaches to the prohibition of soothsaying the promise of a prophet, contrasting what the Lord would do for his people with what he denied them, it is evident from that connection alone that the promise relates neither to one particular prophet nor exclusively to the Messiah, but treats of the sending of prophets generally.
15:
Calvin explains why it stands here. It is added by anticipation, lest the Israelites object that they were more hardly dealt with than the other nations; for communication with God was always justly reckoned an extraordinary blessing, and an opinion had obtained currency that men approached him more closely by magical arts, Pythonic oracles and augury. Moses answers that their access to God would be no less familiar than if he came down from heaven himself, if only they kept the right way and were content with the rule he deemed best.

Who the prophet is divides them more sharply than anything else in the chapter. Gill takes the promise for a single person and rules out the alternatives by name — not Joshua, as Aben Ezra, nor Jeremiah, as Baal Haturim, nor a succession of prophets, as Jarchi — for a single person only is spoken of, and there is a dissimilitude between Moses and any one of the prophets and all of them in succession. It is the Messiah, with whom the whole agrees, and upon this the expectation of a prophet among the Jews was raised. Calvin concludes the opposite from the same words: the singular stands for a number of prophets, and it is altogether absurd to restrict it to Joshua or Jeremiah, since Moses is treating of the continual manner of the Church's government, not of what God would do within a short time — but not at all more correct, he adds, is the opinion of those who apply it strictly to Christ alone, since God's intention was that no excuse be left the Jews if they turned aside to familiar spirits. He finds Isaiah drawing on this passage, asking whether a people should not seek unto their God rather than to them that have familiar spirits, and sending them to the law and to the testimony. Henry holds both readings together. Some think it a promise of a succession of prophets, extraordinary ministers to reprove, remind and forewarn; having these, they need not use divinations, since they might inquire of God's prophets even in private affairs. But whether a succession is included or not, Henry is sure the promise is primarily of Christ, and calls it the clearest promise of him in all the law. Clarke, citing Ainsworth, argues for that side: Christ alone was like Moses as a prophet, since it is written that there arose not a prophet in Israel like unto Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face — which cannot be understood of the ordinary prophets.

On what likeness to Moses amounts to, those who read the verse of Christ are exact. Henry gives three: a prophet great above all the prophets, by whom God would make himself known more fully than ever, the light of the world as prophecy was of the Jewish church; one raised up from the midst of them, in his birth one of that nation and in his resurrection raised at Jerusalem, whence his doctrine went out to all the world; and one like Moses, only as much above him as the other prophets fell short, since Moses was lawgiver and deliverer, and so is Christ, who not only teaches but rules and saves. Clarke lists the offices — prophet, legislator, king, mediator and head of the people of God — and adds that every word he spoke is a living infallible oracle from God. Wesley says he was in all commendable parts like Moses — prophet, king, priest and mediator — in the excellency of his ministry and the glory of his miracles. Gill fills out the prophetic office: mighty in word and deed, foretelling his own sufferings and resurrection and the fall of Jerusalem, but also teaching divine things and speaking as never man did — so that as the law came by Moses, grace and truth came by him.
16:
The promise is grounded in something the people themselves asked for, and Gill supplies the occasion: it answers their request at Horeb, when the law was delivered in the terrible manner it was, and 'in the day of the assembly' means the day the tribes were gathered at the foot of the mount to receive it. Keil and Delitzsch draw the conclusion the grammar invites. With this assurance the Lord had fully granted the request of the people, according to all that they had desired of him; and Israel was therefore all the more bound to hearken to the prophets whom God would raise up from the midst of itself, and not to resort to heathen soothsayers.

Calvin makes the whole passage turn on the usefulness of the fear the people felt that day. In order that the prophetic office might be more reverenced and beloved by them, and lest it should fall into disrepute through their beholding the prophet to be but a mortal, God had extracted from them the confession that nothing could be better than that he should make choice of human interpreters. At the promulgation of the law the visible majesty of God had shone forth, and the people, terrified at the sight, had voluntarily desired that Moses should be given them as a teacher and as the proclaimer of the heavenly voice. Calvin has already remarked how useful that terror was to recommend teaching delivered by the mouth of man, and presses the point on his own readers: we have abundant experience that our minds are carried away by vain speculations, so that we would bring God down from heaven as often as a doubt creeps in. It was necessary, therefore, that the Israelites be convinced of their weakness, lest they go beyond their due bounds; that they be led to ask as a great blessing what God had foreseen to be for their good; and that they abandon the proud curiosity which would always have been exciting them, had it not been corrected betimes by this remedy. From which Calvin draws the charge: they would be guilty of ingratitude if they did not quietly submit themselves to their prophets, since on this very point God had complied with their own request.

The next verse records God's verdict on the request, and Calvin is careful about what that does and does not establish. Moses relates how the desire was approved by the judgment and voice of God — not as if whatever the foolish caprice of men urges them absurdly to ask ought therefore to be granted, but that when God's consent and, so to speak, his vote coincides with a request, whatever he shows to be pleasing to him stands firm and inviolable. Hence it follows that God, in sending the prophets, provided for the salvation of men in the way that was most expedient; and Calvin adds that when pious teachers arise who faithfully show the way of salvation, it is an extraordinary proof of his favour, for which he takes the praise to himself. Calvin's text preserves at this verse an older note on the disputed reference, which reports that some of the Hebrews understand by that prophet Joshua, who succeeded Moses as ruler, while others think Jeremiah must be meant, who rebuked the people in the same terms; but that Christians who assert the passage speaks of Christ confute them by the last chapter of the book, that there arose not a prophet since in Israel like unto Moses. The passage must therefore be prophetic of some other remarkable prophet who should not be inferior to Moses — and, the note adds, as Moses delivered the people from corporal bondage, so shall the prophet whom God will raise up deliver them from the bondage of sin. Gill notes only that it was Moses who had carried the request to the Lord.
18:
Gill notes something easy to miss: it seems from the way the promise is introduced that it was first made at Mount Sinai and is here renewed, though recorded nowhere else. He also draws out what it originally answered. The people were not only made easy for the present by the appointing of Moses to receive all further notices of God's will, but were assured that when it pleased him to make a new revelation he would not do it in the terrible way he had delivered the law, but would raise up one of their own flesh and blood to deliver it — enough to prevent their fears for the future. On the clauses that follow Gill is brief: those who will not hearken slight the doctrines of the Gospel, and the prophet who presumes pretends a commission from God who never sent him. Wesley glosses the sanction and then makes it historical: I will require it means I will punish him severely, and the sad effect of this threatening the Jews have felt for above sixteen hundred years together.

Calvin pauses here to mark a division in the law itself. Thus far, he says, he has reviewed the supplements to the First Commandment relating to the ancient types and to legal worship. That Commandment will always remain in force, even to the end of the world, and is given not only to the Jews but to us also; but God formerly used the ceremonies as temporary aids, whose use has ceased though their utility remains, since from them it more clearly appears how God is to be duly served. Now follow what he calls the political supplements, whereby God commands punishments to be inflicted if his religion has been violated. Calvin defends the principle that a state should legislate this way at all: political laws are not enacted only for earthly affairs, that men may maintain mutual equity and observe what is right, but that they may exercise themselves in the veneration of God. He appeals to a witness outside Scripture, since Plato begins from this very point when he lays down the constitution of a republic, calling the fear of God the preface of all laws; nor, Calvin adds, has any profane author existed who did not confess this the principal part of a well-constituted state, that all with one consent should reverence and worship God.

The chapter then raises, as an unspoken thought, the question how a true prophet is to be known — and Gill observes that this is exactly what it is, a thought arising in the mind, appearing a difficulty, upon which a query is made. Calvin explains why it had to be met. God, in appointing prophets as his substitutes in teaching, had invested them with no common authority, enjoining obedience to their precepts; but those on whom the office of teaching is conferred do not always duly fulfil it, and hence the doubt arises how the people shall determine when they are addressed as by God's mouth, so as to distinguish true from false. No question is expressed in words, but God anticipates the secret scruples which might otherwise keep men's minds in suspense — for to say a thing in the heart is to doubt within oneself when danger is perceived. To remove the difficulty God does not enumerate all the marks of distinction, since he alludes not to doctrine at all but only to prophecies; speaking popularly, as to evil and ignorant persons, he bids them observe whether those who pretend to the name of prophet foretell the truth. And though false teachers rival the servants of God here, and are sometimes found veracious in a particular prophecy, Calvin holds it sufficient as a touchstone to set down what happens for the most part — just as God himself chooses to be distinguished from idols by that same test.
22:
The chapter ends with a single practical test, and Keil and Delitzsch state its force precisely: the false prophet was to be discovered by the fact that the word proclaimed by him did not follow or come to pass, so that by this injunction the occurrence of what had been predicted is made the criterion of true prophecy, and not signs and wonders. Gill adds the one qualification that keeps the rule from being mechanical. If the thing follows not, that is the thing which the Lord has not spoken — as with the prophecy of Hananiah — or otherwise it would have come to pass, unless a condition is either expressed or implied, such as the repentance or the disobedience of a people. Wesley puts the same test in a sentence: the thing is what the prophet gives as a sign of the truth of his prophecy, and the falsehood of his prediction shows him to be a false prophet. Clarke notices a feature of the prophetic writings which makes the test workable, that the prophets in general predicted things which were shortly to come to pass, so that the people might have the fullest proof both of their divine mission and of the existence of God's providence in the administration of the affairs of men. Ellicott alone carries the rule forward into the Gospel, calling it one form of our Lord's test for all prophets, that by their fruits — meaning the results of their teaching, not its first impressions — ye shall know them.

On the word rendered presumptuously the witnesses are unusually vehement. Gill takes it of speaking in a bold and daring manner, with great impiety and impudence, out of the prophet's own head and heart, the thing being a mere device and imagination of his own which, not having the fear of God, he delivered as coming from the Lord. Wesley compresses the same charge into a phrase, impudently ascribing his own vain and lying fancies to the God of truth. Calvin distinguishes two faults in it rather than one. God condemns not only the folly and vanity of those who advance their own inventions in the place of his commands, but also their arrogance; for this is impious and intolerable audacity, to set forth the offspring of man's earthly brain as if it were a divine revelation. And on that ground, he says, their impiety is detestable who fill the air with the fumes of their revelations in order to alarm the simple.

The closing clause tells Israel what to do about such a man, and it is here that the witnesses turn from definition to nerve. Gill reads the command as covering both reproof and punishment: they were not to be afraid of him, either to reprove him for his wickedness or to punish him for it, showing no regard to the high character he assumes nor to the great pretensions he makes to sanctity, knowledge and familiarity with God. Calvin explains why the reassurance was needed at all. Nothing can be more arrogant than the ministers of Satan, and they confidently utter their boastings, by which we may easily be moved and even overwhelmed, unless we had this buckler to protect us — that their terrific noise may be safely despised. He then applies it to his own century without softening it. This doctrine, he says, is nowadays very useful for us: we know how insolently the Papists boast of the Catholic Church and of the Apostolic See, how fiercely they rage in Peter's name, and how impetuously they fulminate their curses and anathemas; but when it is once ascertained that whatever they put forward as revelations of the Spirit are but the empty figments of men, it will be easy to dispel those terrors, which flow from the same fountain of presumption that the law condemns here.
